In summary, five isoindigo quaternary ammonium salt derivatives were synthesized in this paper using isoindigo as the parent body to explore their application as levelers in PCB through-hole plating. The results of electrochemical experiments show that five IID-QAS exhibit diferent degrees of copper deposition inhibition, among which IID-C4-QL has the best inhibition performance and strong convective adsorption ability. Theoretical calculations and molecular simulations show that IID-C4-QL has the strongest adsorption capacity among the five compounds. In the actual copper plating test, the highest TP value of 120.77% can be obtained with the addition of IID-C4-QL at 1.5 ppm, and the SEM results show that IID-C4-QL can obtain the flattest layer at the same concentration, while the addition of more than 1.5 ppm will compete with SPS for adsorption, resulting in the ‘‘cavity phenomenon’’ and decrease of the TP value of the layer. XRD results show that the addition of IID-C4-QL transforms the crystallographic orientation of the copper layer from (220) to the most stable (111) crystallographic plane. The present work enriches the study of isoindigo on this field and exploits the great potential and scope of isoindigo derivatives for acid plating applications.

Based on the research on Tween compounds as eco— friendly suppressors for acid copper electroplating in microvia applications, several key guidelines are proposed. Firstly, when selecting Tween compounds, factors like their hydrophilic—lipophilic balance, molecular weight, and branching structure should be carefully considered to ensure proper adsorption and inhibitory efects. Secondly, concentration optimization is crucial, as both too low and too high concentrations can negatively impact microvia filling quality, thus requiring systematic studies to find the optimal balance. Thirdly, using Tween compounds in combination with other electroplating additives and understanding their synergistic efects can enhance the overall plating performance, although their compatibility and interaction mechanisms need thorough investigation. Finally, environmental considerations are essential, including minimizing compound loss during bath operation and adopting appropriate biodegradation processes for waste treatment. By adhering to these guidelines, Tween compounds can be efectively applied, promoting more sustainable and eficient microelectronics manufacturing, and future research should further explore and optimize their application.

The Cu–O distance to the methoxy group is longer (2.177 $\mathring \mathrm { A } )$ , indicating that the Cu–N interaction is stronger than the Cu–O one. To evaluate the bond nature, we calculated the bond-critical-point (BCP) parameters (Table 1). IRI analysis (Figure 7b) reveals blue isosurfaces between ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ and the tetrazolium nitrogen, as well as between ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ and the methoxy oxygen, indicating strong Cu–N and Cu–O interactions. In this work, we propose a cobalt electrodeposition additive which can be used for superfilling. The inhibition efect of alkyne-PEG4-amine (AP4A) was investigated by electrochemical methods, including cyclic voltammetry and chronopotentiometry. Quantum chemical calculations were applied to confirm the inhibition efect of the AP4A molecule on electrodeposition. The results of the cobalt electrodeposition experiment showed that AP4A has significant influence on electrical properties, surface morphology, and crystal structure. In superfilling of nanometer scale structures with high aspect ratios, the additive AP4A was used to achieve bottom-up cobalt electrodeposition successfully. This study provides a targeted solution for superfilled cobalt plating, which has a good role in promoting the development of electroplating in the future.

Typically, polyether macromolecules (e.g., polyethylene glycol, PEG) serve as suppressors; bridged by chloride ions, they profoundly enhance cathodic polarization and retard copper growth.<sup>14</sup> Sulfonate compounds bearing thiol or disulfide groups (e.g., bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide, SPS) act as accelerators: they capture Cu<sup>2+</sup> at the cathode interface and lower the activation barrier for its reduction.<sup>15</sup> Among the plating formulations, the leveler plays the most critica interfacial regulatory role. By preferentially adsorbing at strongly convected regions (e.g., the opening), the leveler establishes a localized high-impedance barrier that inhibits overplating,<sup>16−18</sup> thereby compelling the spatial electric field lines to redistribute deeper into TH.<sup>19−21</sup> To date, various commercial dyes have been reported as levelers (e.g., Janus Green B, tetrazolium blue chloride, PAN).<sup>22−24</sup> Meanwhile, some researchers have devoted eforts to the synthesis of nove polymeric levelers (e.g., VIBDGE, PBDGE, Sudan-QNL). 25−27 Nevertheless, each of the aforementioned levelers exhibits specific limitations. Polymeric levelers such as VIBDGE and PBDGE, despite their promising performance, typically require multistep synthesis and tedious purification procedures, which considerably increase the production cost and hinder their practical scalability. Commercial dye-based levelers (e.g., Janus Green B) are readily accessible and have been widely adopted in industry with proven efectiveness; however, as the aspec ratio of through-holes continues to increase, further enhance ment of throwing power remains highly desirable to ensure the thickness uniformity and long-term reliability of the copper interconnects. In this regard, MTT ofers a compelling combination of advantages: it is a commercially available, of the-shelf reagent that can be directly procured at low cost entirely eliminating the need for custom synthesis or purification, and as will be demonstrated in Section 3.5, it delivers a throwing power (TP = 96.8%) that markedly outperforms the conventional leveler JGB (TP = 84.5%) under identical bath composition and process conditions. Therefore, a systematic investigation of MTT as a tailored leveler for high aspect-ratio PCB through-hole electroplating is of urgent practical significance.

Huang et al.<sup>33,44</sup> reported the efects of three oxime compounds, dimethylglyoxime (DMG), cyclohexane monoxime (CHO), and cyclohexane dioxime (CHD), on cobalt bottom-up superfilling. Chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM confirm that Copper growth obeys 3D diffusioncontrolled instantaneous nucleation and growth process, with ZPS significantly increasing the density of active sites. A comprehensive theoretical framework combining density functional theory calculations, molecula dynamics simulations, and in situ infrared spectroscopy elucidates an adsorption-capturing acceleration mechanism: ZPS can adsorb on copper surface and “catch” free Cu<sup>2+</sup> to the active sites to accelerate the electrochemical reduction process coupled with adsorbed Cl<sup>−</sup> . Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) further indicates grain refinement (mean size from 3.29 μm to 2.60 μm) and increased twin-boundary density, which contribute to strengthening via Hall-Petch and dislocation-blocking effects. Finite-element simulation of high frequency signal transmission demonstrates that the lowered roughness effectively mitigates the skin effect, reducing signal loss. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive mechanistic understanding of ZPS and dem onstrates its potential as a single additive for producing high-performance electrolytic copper foils.

Leveler is one of the most important additives for super-conformal copper electroplating, which has been widely applied in the fabrication of nanoscale (or microscale) interconnect features in integrated circuits (ICs) and printed circuit boards (PCBs). Because the structure-property relationship of the leveler is not clear, the development of novel leveler with high microvia filling performance is very time-consuming and challenging. In this study, a series of triphenylmethane-based (TPM-based) molecules with different nitrogen-containing groups have been designed, synthesized, and investigated as novel levelers for superconformal copper electroplating. Their structure-property relationships are investigated by electrochemical analyses, contact angle measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments. It is found that the steric hindrance and the type of the nitrogen-containing groups (tertiary amine or quaternary ammonium with counter anions) in a leveler not only affect its adsorption ratio and strength on the copper interface, but also affect its adsorption preference on different copper crystalline plane. In combination with Cl−, polyethylene glycol (PEG, suppressor), and bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS, accelerator), all TPM-based levelers show excellent microvia filling performances in copper electroplating and their effective concentrations are related to their antagonistic ability against the accelerator SPS.

Cobalt electroplating is an efficient and cost-effective method for achieving highquality cobalt interconnects [31,32]. By introducing certain organic additives into the plating solution, bottom-up cobalt superfilling can be realized. Superfilling refers to the phenomenon where the metal deposition rate at the bottom of a trench exceeds that in the side wall. This technique is particularly crucial for the fabrication of interconnects with high aspect ratios, as it effectively prevents the formation of voids, ensuring the integrity and reliability of the interconnects. To date, multiple super-conformal filling mechanisms have been proposed by different research groups. The S-shaped negative differential resistance [33,34] has been extensively applied to the overfilling processes of various metals, including copper [35], gold [36], nickel [37], cobalt [38], and zinc [39]. This model suggests that the adsorption and desorption behavior of inhibitors on the electrode surface leads to a nonlinear variation in current density within a specific potential range, resulting in an “S”-shaped curve. By optimizing inhibitor concentration and potential control, this model enables the realization of the bottom-up overfilling of metals in high-aspect-ratio structures. Rigsby et al. [40,41] introduced the differential current efficiency fill mechanism, emphasizing the critical role of the H<sup>+</sup> concentration gradient in overfilling processes. They observed that during the electrodeposition of cobalt, the pH gradient rapidly formed within the trenches due to proton transfer, resulting in a disparity between the current efficiency and deposition rate at the trench interior and the opening. This differential effect facilitated the bottom-up filling of cobalt. In parallel, Wu et al. [42] introduced the hydrogen reduction-induced deactivation mechanism, which elaborates on how changes in pH and H<sup>+</sup> concentration affect the inhibitory efficacy of additives, thereby triggering a bottom-up filling mechanism. That model showed that the self-initiated bottom-up filling of cobalt was driven by the reduction in and deactivation of inhibitors at the bottom of the trench, caused by hydrogen gas evolution, leading to a diminished inhibitory effect and subsequently promoting the deposition rate at the bottom. The adsorption energy determines the conformality of deposited cobalt layers, especially in complex geometries structures, but its role in achieving superconformal filling has been largely overlooked. Addressing this gap is essential for improving the precision and reliability of coating processes in advanced applications.

Coupling the theoretical elucidation of the MTT inhibition mechanism in Section 3.3 with previous studies, competitive interfacial polarization remodeling driven by a multiphysics coupling mechanism was proposed to unveil the intrinsic influence of MTT. As portrayed in the schematic mechanism (Figure 5c), governed by the coupling of fluid dynamics (convective mass transfer) and electrochemical kinetics, MTT, PEG, and SPS undergo competitive adsorption at the solid− liquid interface within the through-hole. This induces a spatially diferentiated distribution of polarization resistance, reshaping the potential field across the inner surface of the through-hole. Specifically, propelled by the forced convection at the hole opening, MTT rapidly accumulates and adsorbs in this region via convection-dependent adsorption (CDA).<sup>54,55</sup> Concurrently, MTT interacts synergistically with the PEG polymer chains and the bridging chloride ions to form a dense ternary synergistic suppression film on the copper substrate. This compact adsorption layer triggers a notable increase in the local polarization resistance at the opening. The resulting elevated electrochemical reaction barrier efectively suppresses the electroreduction kinetics of ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ in this vicinity. Consequently, the increased polarization resistance at the orifice compels the spatial electric field lines $( \mathrm { i . e . , }$ the primary current distribution) to redistribute toward the deep interior of the through-hole, which is situated in a weak convection zone.<sup>56,57</sup> Through this polarization remodeling efect, the inherent Ohmic potential drop caused by the geometric aspect ratio of the through-hole is compensated. Simultaneously, a steady-state difusion flux of $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ directed into the hole is sustained, ultimately driving the realization of a conformal through-hole deposition.

Blind hole copper electroplating is the primary technology used in the connectivity manufacturing process for printed circuit boards (PCB), semiconductor integrated circuit (IC) chips, and IC packaging substrates [1–3]. The issue of achieving complete filling of high-quality plated copper has become increasingly essential in light of the progress made in integrated and miniaturized electronic devices. This is particularly relevant as high-density interconnect printed circuit boards (PCBs) are transitioning towards through-hole and micro-hole designs with larger depth-to-diameter ratios [4]. In the process of copper plating on such PCB micro vias with a larger depth-to-diameter ratio, there is a very significant difference between a current’s density distribution inside and on the surface of the micro vias. In such an environment, the copper electrodeposition rate in the pore area will be significantly greater than that in the micropores’ bottom region, which will result in the coppe layer covering and sealing the pore area in a preferential manner, leading to internal defects in the pores. In order to achieve bottom-up superfilling of the micropores, a synergistic effect of different addi tives is required, namely accelerators, inhibitors, levelling agents and chloride ions. Accelerators are generally small molecule organic sul phides containing specific functional groups of (-S–S-), sulfhydryl (-SH) and sulphonic acid $\left( - S O _ { 3 ^ { - } } \right)$ groups, which typically preferentially adsorb at the micropore’s bottom and can hasten the electrodeposition of copper at the hole’s bottom. SPS and MPS are both common accelerator $[ 5 , 6 ]$ . During copper electrodeposition, the inhibitor is usually adsorbed on the cathode surface and interacts with chloride ions to increase the overpotential, thereby achieving the inhibitory effect on the surface deposition of copper, Inhibitors are mainly macromolecular polyether or polyols [7]. The most prevalent inhibitors are polyethylene glycol (PEG), but in addition to PEG there are also polypropylene glycol (PPG) and triblock copolymers of PEG and PPG [8–10]. Levelling agents can be added in very small amounts compared to inhibitors to achieve a strong inhibiting effect and rapid deactivation, leaving the surface flat and smooth. Meantime, levelling agents also show an inhibiting effect o copper deposition but there is no substitute for inhibitors, which can be compared to short-acting inhibitors, while inhibitors show a moderate inhibiting effect and deactivate slowly, and throughout the plating process, the levelling agent gradually covers the copper surface, domi nating the completion of superconformal deposition [4,7]. Traditiona levelling agents such as Janus Green B (JGB), Diazine Black (DB) Methylene Blue (MB), Alsin Blue (ABPV) [11–14]. However, these dye conventional levelling agents are prone to decomposition at high tem peratures, which makes the plating process not easy to control increasing the cost and also leading to copper plating quality problems. In response to the above problems, researchers have continued t develop new environmentally friendly high-performance small molecul copper plating levelling agents, such as benzyl quaternary ammonium containing compounds phenylacetyl chloride (BZC) [15], 2,2-dithiodi pyridine (DTDP) [16], 4,6-dimethyl-2-mercaptopyrimidine (DMP) [17], tricyclazole (TCA) [18], 1-(4-hydroxyphenyl)-2-tetrazole-5-thion (HPTT) [19]. ## 3.3. Theoretical Insights into the Inhibition Mechanism

The additives used in copper electroplating fall into three categories: accelerators, suppressors, and levelers.<sup>16</sup> The most commonly used accelerator, suppressor, and leveler is bis-(sodium sulfopropyl)- disulfide (SPS), polyethylene glycol (PEG), and Janus Green B (JGB).<sup>17</sup> During electroplating, density functional theory (DFT) calculations, in situ Raman spectroscopy, and scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) studies reveal that the disulfide bond of SPS will break up, with the sulfurcontaining side adsorbing on the copper base, while the other side (containing a sulfonic acid group) captures free $\operatorname { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ to accelerate reduction with adsorbed Cl<sup>-</sup> through the ‘‘bridging efect’’.<sup>18–20</sup> As for PEG, in situ Raman and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations confirm the formation of $\mathbf { P E G - C u ^ { 2 + } - C l ^ { - } }$ adsorbate complexes, which increase the energy barrier and suppress copper electrodeposition.<sup>21–23</sup> Mass spectrometry (MS) and DFT calculations demonstrate that the azo group of JGB competes with the reduction of $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ to obtain electrons, leading to dissociation<sup>24,25</sup> into phenazine derivatives that can also adsorb on active sites to suppress copper growth.<sup>26,27</sup> Among these additives, levelers are key components for achieving defect-free filling in blind vias.<sup>28</sup> Nowadays, triphenylmethane derivatives are promising levelers and have been used in throughhole and blind-hole filling due to the unlocalized orbital distribution of the tertiary amine structure.<sup>29,30</sup>

In order to achieve the bottom-up filling efect without defects in the through-hole, the main option is to add functional additives during copper deposition,<sup>9</sup> which are usually classified into three categories according to the functions they perform in copper plating: inhibitors, levelers and accelerators.<sup>10–13</sup> Inhibitors are mainly polyether compounds, such as polyethylene glycol (PEG), polypropylene glycol (PPG), and most of the large organic molecules with their molecular weights in the range of 6000–10 000, which mainly inhibit the deposition of copper.<sup>14,15</sup> The most common accelerator is sodium polydithiodipropane sulphonate (SPS), which is able to synergize with chloride ions to increase the rate of copper deposition and refine the copper crystalline particles, resulting in a bright copper coating.<sup>16,17</sup> Levelers are the most complex of the additives and a special kind of inhibitor, which can further enhance the dispersing ability of the plating solution and the flatness of the copper layer.<sup>18,19</sup> A series of dye-based levelers with large conjugation planes, such as diketopyrrolopyrrole derivatives, anthraquinone derivatives, 3,3<sup>0</sup>-bicarbazole derivatives, etc., have been reported in previous works of our group,<sup>2,20,21</sup> and it is hypothesized that molecules possessing good planarity as well as large conjugation are better at leveling.

Electroplating is a critical technology in high-end electronic manufacturing, including integrated circuits. As interconnect dimensions continue to shrink, copper electroplating is increasingly unable to meet the required performance and safety standards. Cobalt, with its superior electrical properties and safety at the micro-/nanoscale, is emerging as a promising next-generation interconnect material to replace copper. Although there have been reports on cobalt electroplating, current research has primarily focused on the electrochemical behavior of cobalt ions and additives, the role of additives, and the filling efects in trenches and vias, along with proposed filling mechanisms. However, several key aspects remain insuficiently explored. These include the specific actions and synergistic/antagonistic interactions of components such as boric acid and additives in the plating bath, the mechanisms by which pH, temperature, and individual bath components influence cobalt nucleation and growth, and the surface, interface, and filling processes during cobalt electrodeposition in micro-/nanostructures. Future research directions should prioritize the development and application of advanced in situ techniques, including morphological, spectroscopic, and energy spectroscopic, to address these challenges. Clarifying these mechanisms will be essential for advancing cobalt electroplating as a viable interconnect technology in next-generation chip fabrication.

To conclude, size is one of the key parameters influencing any catalyst’s catalytic performance, especially transition metalsbased nanocatalysts in different chemical reactions [102]. Its influence is complicated in many cases, such as if the rate-determining step is the dissociation of an intra-molecular bond of a reactant molecule, then it is expected that the metal atom has a lower coordination number and exhibits higher catalytic activity [103–109]. Metal atoms with smaller coordination numbers on the surface have stronger adsorption energy, which could reduce the activation barrier to dissociate the reactant molecules and hence accelerate the catalytic process. The size-dependent catalytic activity is favored when the dissociation step acts as the rate-determining step. While in some cases, this trend is opposite to the above statement, in that case, the metal surface atoms have lower coordination numbers, dramatically dissociate a chemical bond, and tightly bind the dissociated species. Transition metal (TM) catalyzed cross-coupling reactions are the utmost versatile and reliable methods for the production of many industrially important fine chemicals. The utilization of transition metals nanocatalysts in organic transformations, specifically the Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions, have enticed the vigilant eye of researchers and technologists due to; (i) high surface area, (ii) higher number of surface atoms leading to large number of catalytic active centers, and (iii) chemical stability. Moreover, being colloidal, nanomaterials combine the properties of both homogeneous and heterogeneous. i.e., solubility in different solvents and ease in the separation of catalysts. This improves the overall catalytic efficiency and cost. Therefore, these pseudo-homogeneous nanocatalysts are gaining a great deal of attention due to their broad substrate scope and ease of handling. This review article focuses on the recent advances in developing nanostructured catalysts and their utilization for selective carbon–carbon bond-forming reactions, e.g., Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira coupling reactions. The main focus is laid on the reactions catalyzed by nanocatalysts derived from transition metals such as Pd, Pt, Cu, Ag, Ni, Fe, Au, and Zn, expounding the conception and rationale based on the reactivity improvement and the recyclability of the nanocatalysts are presented here. The heterogeneous catalysis, essential in daily chemical transformations, is demonstrated, implicating significant functions presented by the nanocatalysts, related pros and cons, recyclability, and efficiency.

Cobalt electrodeposition is the core technology in chip manufacturing. Butynediol (BD) is the key component in cobalt electrodeposition. Abstract: Levelers, as an essential part of organic additives in copper electroplating, play a crucial role in the fabrication of sophisticated interconnects in integrated circuits, packaging substrates, and printed circuit boards. In this work, four N-heterocyclic oligomers were synthesized and characterized, along with investigations of their electrochemical behaviors and their synergism with other bath components. The corresponding effects of the oligomers on the deposited copper films were analyzed by morphological and compositional characterizations. The leveling mechanism of the oligomers was further discussed with the aid of quantum chemical calculations. The results exhibit that each of these N-heterocyclic oligomers holds a particular degree of leveling ability. The oligomer of 1,3-bis(1-imidazolyl)propane and 1,3-dichloro-2-propanol (IPIEP) is the best leveler for THs plating compared with the other three oligomers. It was found that the hydroxyl group in IPIEP enhances the hydrophilicity of the modified molecule and triggers a more stable complexation between IPIEP and H O−Cu(I)−MPS. Moreover, imidazole demonstrates a better practicality than piperazine. This work recommends the combination of N-heterocycles in planar conformation with modification by the hydroxyl group to synthesize high-performance straight-chain levelers

Chloride ions enhance the conductivity of the system, facilitate the dissolution of phosphor copper anodes, reduce the formation of “copper powder” due to incomplete anode dissolution, improve the brightness and leveling ability of the coating, and enhance coating quality. However, there are three main issues associated with the research on leveling agents both domestically and internationally. First, current research mostly uses theoretical calculations, electrochemical methods, and electroplating experiments to investigate the mechanisms and efects of electroplating additives. Unlike traditional electrodeposition, chip copper interconnection involves precise deposition in a narrow space or surface at the micronano level. The morphology and uniformity of the copper deposition layer have a direct impact on the electrical performance of the copper interconnection line, thereby influencing the overall chip performance.<sup>14,15</sup> Its characteristics mainly include small electroplating dimensions, dificulty in filling microholes with uneven current density, and high coating quality requirements. However, there is a distinct lack of comprehensive research on electroplating with structured wafers, which renders most research results unable to be applied in practice. Second, copper sulfate electroplating leveling agents are primarily composed of dye organic polymers such as JGB, which tend to generate significant pollution. With the development of wafer-level, system-level, and 3D packaging, the performance ofelectroplating additives is facing increased scrutiny and evaluation. As a result, the industry is urgently requiring the development of novel electroplating leveling agents. Third, the majority of the existing research is focused on developing independent research models for wafer surface wiring and through-hole filling. However, in practical IC manufacturing, through-hole filling and wiring are performed concurrently, which causes a gap between study findings and application.<sup>16−18</sup> Therefore, it is crucial to develop an application-based screening and evaluation strategy for electroplating additives.

The main difficulty in copper filling is the formation of voids in TH with higher aspect ratio due to the uneven local current distribution and tanglesome convection environments caused by the specific geometry of TH [15–17]. The copper deposition amount at the mouth is usually higher than that at the center of TH, resulting in the coating in a void or seam. Therefore, it is particularly crucial introducing the organic additives in the acidic sulfate bath to modulate the copper deposition process at the mouth and center. The key to blind hole filling is the bottom-up growth of copper coating. The key to TH filling is that copper coating rapidly deposits at the center of TH wall until the center is connected to form a butterfly shape structure (two blind holes), and then the two blind holes are filled separately. The accelerator of bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) and suppressor of polyethylene glycol (PEG) are the commonly used additives in the acidic sulfate bath [18–25]. Suppressor, mainly distributed at the mouth of TH, inhibits the copper ion electro-reduction at a definite potential which results in the decrease of reduction current density. Accelerator, mainly distributed at the center of $\mathrm { T H } ,$ promotes the copper ion electro-reduction at a definite potential which results in the increase of reduction current density. It is still difficult to realize a void-free copper filling from the bath with only these two additives, and therefore the other additive is further needed. Zheng et al. [12] reported that poly (1-vinyl imidazole co 1, 4-butanediol diglycidyl ether) (VIBDGE) could further heighten the inhibiting ability of PEG in copper electronic plating. Li et al. [13] presented that a copolymer comprising of pyrrole and 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether (PBDGE) also could enhance the inhibiting ability of PEG during copper electronic plating. Wang et al. [14] introduced that gentian violet (GVT) behaved with the synergistic inhibiting effect with PEG and the antagonistic effect with SPS. Although considerable studies have been carried out to show the superior performance of additives, up to now, the synergistic action mechanisms of additives are still not clarified.

The electron mean free path of copper is 39 nm.<sup>18</sup> Generally, the larger the electron mean free path of the bulk metal, the lower the resistivity of the metal. When the characteristic size of interconnects is reduced to the electron mean free path of copper, the electrons inside the copper are subjected to strong grain boundary scattering and interface scattering, causing a sudden increase in resistivity. Compared with copper, cobalt has a smaller electron mean free path (about 10 nm);<sup>18</sup> that is, cobalt possesses a smaller size efect than copper.<sup>19</sup> When the trench critical dimension is above about 7 nm, copper wires have lower resistivity. When the trench critical dimension is below about 7 nm, cobalt wires exhibit even lower resistivity.<sup>20</sup> The resistivities of diferent widths for Cu and Co are shown in Fig. 3. In electrochemical measurements, cyclic voltammetric curves were performed to test the ability of organics to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions in the electroplating solution. The negative current density peak in the cyclic voltammetric curve was the copper deposition peak, which represented the ability of copper ions to be reduced to copper and deposited. While, the positive current density peak was the copper stripping peak, whose area represented the ability of the deposited copper to be oxidized to copper ions. The peak area of the copper stripping peak was positively correlated with the peak area of the copper deposition peak. Therefore, the smaller the peak of the copper deposition peak, the smaller the peak area of the copper stripping peak, which implied the stronger ability of the organics to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions [29,46].
